items.scene: Maya is reading at a desk. A bright red mug sits in clear view on the table next to her notebook.
items.question: Can Maya directly perceive the red mug through vision?
options: Yes, the mug is visually available to her
No, because she is not looking at it
No, because she only hears it described
items.why_this_case_matters: Tests direct sensory access even when attention is elsewhere.

items.scene: Jon hears a crash from the kitchen and sees broken glass on the floor after he walks in.
items.question: Did Jon directly perceive that the vase hit the floor?
options: Yes, he directly saw the vase hit the floor
No, he only inferred it from the broken glass and crash
Yes, because he heard a crash
No, because broken glass cannot be seen
items.why_this_case_matters: Separates direct perception from inference from clues.

items.scene: Nina is in another room when her brother says, 'The cookie jar is empty.' She never goes to the kitchen.
items.question: Did Nina directly perceive the jar's contents?
options: Yes, because she heard the statement
Yes, because she can imagine the jar
No, she only received a report about it
No, because hearing is never a sensory channel

items.scene: While standing outside a closed apartment door, Priya smells smoke coming from inside and assumes the stove is on fire.
items.question: Did Priya directly perceive that there was a fire on the stove?
options: Yes, the smoke smell gives direct access to the fire itself
No, she only perceived smoke and inferred the fire
Yes, because she can smell anything inside the apartment
No, because smell is not a valid sensory channel
items.why_this_case_matters: Targets the shortcut of treating a sensory cue as access to the hidden fact.
